title: The Holocaust, honestly
hookLine: Catholics were among the rescuers, the bystanders and the perpetrators, and the Church's document We Remember asked for repentance

cards: A question from the first family in Genesis. Cain has killed his brother, and God asks him where Abel is. Cain answers with a question of his own, in the Douay-Rheims: "am I my brother's keeper?"

During the Holocaust, when Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered Europe's Jews, that question was answered town by town, by all kinds of people. Baptized Catholics were among the people who answered it.
Some answered yes, at the cost of their lives. Some looked away. And some were the killers.
Today is not a saint's story. It's an honest one.

teach.b: Four honest things. First, the rescuers. Priests, sisters, farmers and families hid Jewish neighbors in convents, attics and barns, forged papers, and carried children to safety.
Some were caught and killed for it. In a few days we'll meet one of them by name.
Second, the bystanders. Others did nothing. They saw neighbors taken away and stayed quiet, out of fear, or indifference, or a habit of thinking of Jews as other.
Third, the perpetrators. Some who carried out the murders had been baptized, sat in pews, and took communion. Nothing in their faith stopped them.

teach.h: WE REMEMBER: A CALL TO REPENT.
teach.b: The Vatican later published a document called We Remember: A Reflection on the Shoah. Shoah is the Hebrew word for catastrophe, a word Jewish people use for the Holocaust.
The document says, in its own words, that the Church deeply regrets the failures of her sons and daughters in that time, and calls that an act of repentance.
It also names a long history of anti-Jewish teaching and feeling among Christians, and says that it left some Christians less ready to resist.
Some Jewish readers welcomed the document; some said it did not go far enough, especially on the Church's leaders in those years. Both reactions are part of the record.
The document's title is a promise: to remember, so that the seeds of anti-Judaism and antisemitism are never again allowed to take root.

how: Some Catholic parishes and schools mark Holocaust Remembrance Day with prayer, survivor testimony and joint services with Jewish communities, and the Church's documents on Catholic-Jewish relations are studied in seminaries.

games.q: a Jewish neighbor knocks on your door at night and asks to hide. you know the penalty if you're caught. what do you do?
o: open the door and hide them.
say you can't, and close the door.
games.why: baptized Catholics made all three choices. the rescuers opened the door, and some were killed for it. the Church's own document asks Catholics to remember what was done, and what was not.

practice: Let the word survivor sit with you: a real person who lived through it, with a name, a face, and a life afterward.

If you've heard one survivor's story, in a book, a talk, a recording, or from a relative, bring it back now and stay with that one person; if not, simply hold the people who lived it. If you pray, pray for them and for the dead.

wordCard.voice: The Holocaust. The murder of Europe's Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. In Hebrew, the Shoah. Catholics were among its rescuers, its bystanders and its killers.

orig.note: Hebrew: catastrophe, destruction. the word in the title of the Vatican's document We Remember: A Reflection on the Shoah.

carryVoice: Your line: we remember. Rescuers, bystanders, killers: all of it, honestly. Go gently, and see you tomorrow.
